summary.text: 方 is used today for “square” and “region; local.” Shang inscriptions attest it in directional and polity contexts. Its early graph has been interpreted as a marked blade or other implement, among other proposals; the later paired-boats explanation is a dictionary interpretation, and the original referent remains disputed.

formation.text: The proposed origin analyses treat 方 as a whole pictorial graph, but disagree about the object depicted: suggestions include a marked blade or tool, other implements, and paired boats. No internal component analysis is supported. One account proposes that the graph was borrowed to write “square” because the word sounded like the name of the depicted object; that name and sound match are unknown, so the explanation remains unverified.

components.text: 方 is treated as one whole graph in the proposed pictorial analyses. Its early referent is disputed, and the evidence does not support splitting it into meaningful internal parts.

history.text: The curated oracle-script-style image shows an early graphic candidate, but its shape does not settle what it depicts. The paired-boats explanation belongs to a later dictionary tradition, illustrated by the seal-script-style image, and does not establish the graph’s original referent.

Oracle and bronze forms are described as broadly similar, with variation in their upper strokes. A later account describes changes in the seal form and identifies clerical writing as the basis for later forms; it characterizes the seal form’s development as mistaken transformation but does not show that every graphic difference was a corruption.

uncertainties.text: The proposed object remains disputed among blade-, tool-, implement-, paddle-, and boat-related interpretations. Its original name and pronunciation are not established, so a proposed borrowing of 方 for “square” based on sound similarity remains hypothetical.

The reported early and later uses do not establish a dated sequence connecting direction, polity or region, square, method, and temporal “just/now.” Individual early examples lack precise dates in the supplied evidence.
A proposed connection with 旁 does not establish that 方 was its original graph or that the words share meaning; the reported historical sound similarity supports only a possible phonetic relation.

senses.gloss: direction, including west and the four quarters
senses.text: Reported Shang inscription uses include a western-direction context and 四方. These attestations establish early directional use, but do not show whether it continues the graph’s original meaning or reflects borrowing for a similar-sounding word.
Reported Shang examples use 方 for polities and polity leaders. Their relationship to the directional use is not established.

A Western Zhou bronze example is reported with the square sense. One analysis proposes that the graph was reused to write “square” because that word sounded like the name of the depicted object. The name and sound match are unknown, so the borrowing account remains unverified.
A Western Zhou bronze example is reported for land measurement; its relation to the square, direction, or polity senses is not established.
Later lexicographic records include method and law. The evidence does not date their emergence or securely connect them to earlier attested uses.
A period-labeled bronze example is glossed “just/now.” The evidence does not establish its development from another sense.

senses.period: late Warring States to early Qin context
senses.text: A Shuihudi Qin slip is reported to use 方 for a writing board. No semantic link to the other senses is established.
These are supplied modern glosses; their listing does not establish when or how each sense developed.

developments.text: Both uses are reported in Shang material, but the evidence does not show whether the polity use developed from the directional sense or whether the graph was borrowed to write a similar-sounding word.

One analysis proposes that the graph was reused for “square” because that word sounded like the name of the depicted object. Since the name and sound comparison are unknown, the proposed borrowing and its timing remain unverified.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish a complete semantic chronology or connect the recorded square, measurement, region, method, and temporal senses into a single chain.
The earliest depicted object and any borrowing based on its name remain unresolved; the supplied historical pronunciations are readings of 方, not records of the depicted object’s name.

overview.text: Today 方 commonly means “square” or “region; local.” Shang inscriptions also use it for directions and polities. One proposal says it was reused for “square” because the unknown name of the pictured object sounded like that word; the match is unverified.

components.text: Treat 方 as one whole graph: proposed readings picture different objects, and the evidence does not support a breakdown into smaller parts.

takeaway.text: The proposed link between the graph and “square” depends on a possible sound match with the unknown name of the depicted object.
